sections.title: How does the Triangular prism calculator work?
sections.html:
The Triangular prism calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports prism length (L) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the triangle type); then you type in the base (b), the height (h), the side length a (2) and the angle γ (2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Triangular prism calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Prism length (L)=2 × prism volume ÷ (base (b) × height (h))
Side length b=the square root of ((side length a ^ 2) + (side length c ^ 2) + 2 × the square root of ((side length a ^ 2) × (side length c ^ 2) − 4 × (prism volume ^ 2) ÷ (prism length (L) ^ 2)))
Angle γ=(2 × prism volume ÷ (side length a × side length b × prism length (L)))
Angle β=PI
Prism surface area=(((prism length (L) ^ 2) × (side length a + side length b + side length c) + 2 × prism volume) ÷ prism length (L))
Prism surface area=(((prism length (L) ^ 2) × (side length a + side length b + the square root of ((side length a ^ 2) − 2 × side length a × side length b × the cosine of (angle γ) + (side length b ^ 2))) + 2 × prism volume) ÷ prism length (L))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Triangular prism calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the base, the height and the side length a — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Triangular prism calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns prism length (L), derived from the base, the height and the side length a. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Triangular prism calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the base, the height, the side length a and the angle γ, which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter base (b) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Base (b) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Triangular prism calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
